Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Famous trade name: Keppra

Broad spectrum antiepileptic and one of the most commonly prescribed antiepileptics because it has less adverse effects

Levetiracetam was first approved for medical use in 1999 in US for treatment of epilepsy

Mechanism of action

Levetiracetam binds to SV2A protein and Inhibits it

SV2A is a synaptic vesicle membrane proteins, SV2A function is to help in the process of exocytosis of the excitatory neurotransmitters into the synapse

inhibiting SV2A by the levetiracetam lead to less excitatory neurotransmitters released to the synapse

Therapeutic uses

Broad spectrum antiepileptic activity

Can be used as monotherapy or as an add on

It’s FDA approved for:

Focal seizures in adults and children

Idiopathic generalized onset tonic clonic seizures

Myoclonic seizures of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in adolescents older than 12

It is used off label for:

Status epilepticus

For prophylaxis against seizures in subarachnoid hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, palliative care

Adverse effects

CNS: ataxia

Dizziness

Lack of energy

It also lead to leukopenia, eosinophilia and rarely pancytopenia

Less commonly may lead to behavioral and mood changes such as irritability, aggression, agitation, anger, psychosis, anxiety, depression and emotional liability

Rarely lead to hypersensitivity reactions in form of spreading rash progressing to SJS and TEN

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral and intravenous formulations

Rapidly absorbed from the GI tract with 95% bioavailability, food slows absorption but doesn’t affect amount absorbed

Distribution: the drug is protein bound by 10%, the rest is distributed to body tissues

30% of the drug is metabolized by enzymatic hydrolysis of acetamide group in the blood (the liver has minimal role) and the rest excreted unchanged in urine

Plasma half life is around 7 hours

Dosing

IV is the same as oral dose

There is no loading dose

Adult dosing: start with 500 mg twice daily and titrate up until response occur, titration every two weeks by 250-500 mg and max dose is 3000 mg

Pediatrics: used in children older than 5 years, start with 20mg/kg per divided into 2 doses and titrate up by 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks, max dose is 60 mg/kg

Drug interactions

Minimal drug interactions
